Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

quarrel verb

also argue, squabble, bicker, have a row, fall out, wrangle

classical

Plaut. Cas. 317: quīcum lītigās, Olympiō?
Cic. Att. 13.37.2: Hirtium cum Quīnctiō ācerrimē lītigāsse (Lewis & Short)

lītigō, lītigāre, lītigāvī, lītigātum

verb, first conjugation

quarrel, dispute; also go to law

From līs and agō.

Other words

  • jūrgō, jūrgāre, jūrgāvī, jūrgātum — quarrel, wrangle; scold

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Ter. And. 2.3.15: cedo, quid jūrgābit tēcum? (Lewis & Short); Cic. Rep. 4.8: jūrgāre igitur lēx putat inter sē vīcīnōs, nōn lītigāre (Lewis & Short)

    The milder word: Cicero says neighbours jūrgant, they do not lītigant.

  • rixor, rixārī, rixātus sum — brawl, come to blows or hard words

    verb, first conjugation, deponent · also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 2.240: cum esset cum eō dē amīculā rixātus (Lewis & Short); Hor. Ep. 1.18.15: dē lānā caprīnā (Lewis & Short)

Examples

  • Quid istuc est? quīcum lītigās, Olympiō? — Cum eādem quā tū semper.

    What’s this? Who are you quarrelling with, Olympio? — With the same woman you always are.Plaut. Cas. 317–318

  • Quid est? quā dē rē lītigātis nunc inter vōs?

    What is it? What are you two quarrelling about now?Plaut. Rud. 1060

See also argument, tell off, make up.

SourcesLewis & Short: litigo · Lewis & Short: jurgo · Lewis & Short: rixor

Plautus, Casina 317–318; Rudens 1060.
